title: Poker Hand Rank
description: Classify a 5-card poker hand into its category. Parse `rank+suit` strings, build a rank histogram, check straight + flush flags, then walk the ranking ladder from royal-flush downward.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the input format and the output categories.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: I get a 5-card poker hand as an array of strings like `'KH'` or `'10S'`, and I return the category name as a string — `'royal-flush'`, `'straight-flush'`, `'four-of-a-kind'`, `'full-house'`, `'flush'`, `'straight'`, `'three-of-a-kind'`, `'two-pair'`, `'pair'`, or `'high-card'`. Quick clarifying questions:"

• Card format — `'10H'` for ten of hearts (two-char rank), or `'TH'` (single char)? Affects how I parse.
• Always exactly 5 cards? (Variants like 7-card stud find the best 5-card hand from 7.)
• Wheel straight — does A-2-3-4-5 count as a straight? (Standard yes, but worth confirming.)
• Royal flush — separate category, or just the highest straight-flush? (Standard: separate.)
• Tie-breaking — do I need to return the kicker / high card for ranking two hands? (Out of scope for category only.)
sections.why: The card-format question is the load-bearing one for parsing — '10' as two chars means `c.slice(0, -1)` returns '10', which is multi-char and breaks any single-char indexing scheme. Normalizing '10' to 'T' early is the canonical fix; asking the question signals you anticipated the gotcha. The wheel-straight question is the classic edge-case probe — most rule books include it, but interviewers sometimes scope it out to simplify.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious shape before optimizing.
sections.say:
"There's no real 'brute force vs. optimization' here because the input is bounded — 5 cards, at most 52 unique card values, so even the dumbest implementation is O(1). What I want to avoid instead is the *fragile* version: a giant chain of nested-loop boolean checks like 'count quadruples by iterating pairs of pairs of pairs.' That code is hard to read and easy to get wrong.

The cleaner shape: do ONE pass over the cards to extract three independent features — a rank histogram, a flush flag, a straight flag — then walk a top-down ladder of `if` checks that maps feature combinations to categories."
sections.why: Framing this as 'avoid the fragile nested version, prefer the feature-extraction shape' is the right move because the problem doesn't have an interesting time complexity — the complexity question is structural, not algorithmic. Saying 'O(1) because the hand is bounded' first gets that out of the way; the real interview signal is whether you can decompose the problem cleanly. Showing the decomposition (3 features + 1 ladder) is what gets graded.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.say:
"This is a classification ladder backed by a frequency histogram. The pattern: parse rank + suit, then derive three independent features:"

1. **Group histogram** — `counts = {rank: frequency}`. Sort values descending. `[4,1]` = four-of-a-kind, `[3,2]` = full-house, `[3,1,1]` = trips, `[2,2,1]` = two-pair, `[2,1,1,1]` = pair, `[1,1,1,1,1]` = none. This single sorted-values array distinguishes every group-based category.

2. **Flush** — `suits.every(s => s === suits[0])`. One bit.

3. **Straight** — sort the rank-indices, check each is one more than the previous. Special case: the wheel (A-2-3-4-5) needs an explicit override because A's index is 12, not -1.

"Then the ladder, checked top-down: royal-flush → straight-flush → four → full-house → flush → straight → three → two-pair → pair → high-card. TOP-DOWN matters because a full-house ALSO matches three-of-a-kind (and a pair); returning the stronger category first is what makes the ladder correct."
sections.why: Naming the three features as INDEPENDENT and then composing them via the ladder is the load-bearing insight. A candidate who tries to write one giant nested `if` ends up with 9 deeply-nested branches and bugs. Spelling out the sorted-counts array specifically (`[4,1]`, `[3,2]`, `[2,2,1]`) is the trick that collapses 5 different group-counting checks into one sort + one comparison. The top-down ordering is the second test — getting it wrong means a full-house is reported as three-of-a-kind.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk three hands to confirm the model.
sections.intro: "Let me trace three representative hands — a royal flush to hit the top of the ladder, a wheel straight to exercise the ace-low override, and a full house to show how `groups = [3,2]` short-circuits the ladder at the right spot."

examples.note: Top of the ladder — every flag positive, plus the T-A range.
examples.trace:
ranks=['T','J','Q','K','A'] (normalize 10→T)
suits=['S','S','S','S','S']
idx=[8,9,10,11,12] (positions in '23456789TJQKA')
counts={T:1,J:1,Q:1,K:1,A:1} → groups=[1,1,1,1,1]
flush: every suit==='S' → true
straight: idx all consecutive → true
ladder: straight && flush && idx[0]===8 (T's position) → 'royal-flush' ✓ (first ladder check fires)

examples.note: Wheel straight — indices are NOT consecutive (A is at 12, not -1); the explicit override is what saves it.
examples.trace:
ranks=['A','2','3','4','5']
suits=['H','D','S','C','H'] (mixed → not flush)
idx=[0,1,2,3,12] (2,3,4,5 at front; A at 12)
groups=[1,1,1,1,1]
flush: false
straight: idx.every consecutive? 0,1,2,3,12 — false (12 != 3+1)
WHEEL OVERRIDE: ranks include A,2,3,4,5 → straight = true
ladder: not royal/straight-flush (no flush), not four/full/three/two/pair (groups=[1,1,1,1,1]), flush=false → falls through to `straight` → 'straight' ✓

examples.note: groups=[3,2] is THE diagnostic for full-house. Ladder also matches three-of-a-kind and pair downstream — top-down ordering is what makes the correct one win.
examples.trace:
ranks=['K','K','K','2','2']
suits=['H','D','S','H','D'] (mixed → not flush)
idx=[0,0,11,11,11] (sorted: 2,2,K,K,K)
counts={K:3, 2:2} → groups=[3,2] sorted desc
flush: false
straight: 0,0,11,11,11 not consecutive → false
ladder: skip royal/straight-flush, skip four (groups[0]=3 not 4), groups[0]===3 && groups[1]===2 → 'full-house' ✓ (would also match three-of-a-kind two checks later, but ladder fired earlier)

sections.why: The wheel-straight trace is the load-bearing one — it exposes WHY the override exists. Without it, `idx=[0,1,2,3,12]` fails the consecutive check, and you'd misreport A-5 as high-card. The full-house trace defends the top-down ordering — note that `groups=[3,2]` ALSO satisfies `groups[0]===3` (three-of-a-kind, two ladder entries below). Returning at the first match is what makes the higher category win. If you reordered the ladder, you'd get wrong answers.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges worth flagging:"

• Wheel straight (A-2-3-4-5) — ace is low here; without an explicit override, the index check (12 vs. 3+1) fails and you misclassify as high-card. Hand-checked above.
• Royal flush — A-K-Q-J-T of one suit. Just an A-high straight-flush; whether you call it 'royal-flush' or roll it into 'straight-flush' depends on the contract. The standard contract treats it as a separate top category, so it must be checked BEFORE straight-flush.
• Two-pair vs three-of-a-kind — both have a leading `groups[0]` element, but the histogram shape disambiguates: `[2,2,1]` is two-pair, `[3,1,1]` is three. The `groups[0]===3` check is what separates them in the ladder.
• Full-house vs three-of-a-kind — both have `groups[0]===3`. Full-house also has `groups[1]===2`. Check the more-specific full-house pattern first (top-down ordering).
• Card format ambiguity — `'10H'` is 3 chars while every other card is 2. `c.slice(0, -1)` returns '10', which is multi-char. Normalize to 'T' upfront or every subsequent indexing op needs a special case.
• Duplicate cards — undefined behavior in real poker (impossible with one deck). If the input might contain duplicates by mistake, the histogram still gives a meaningful count, but it's worth flagging that two `KH`s would give `groups=[2,...]` and be misreported as a pair.
• Empty / wrong-length hand — `cards.length !== 5` should probably throw or return a sentinel. Worth confirming with the interviewer.
sections.why: The wheel-straight and the full-house-vs-three-of-a-kind cases are the two correctness traps that catch most candidates. Calling them out unprompted shows you've thought past the obvious cases. The card-format ambiguity is the parser-level edge — getting it wrong silently corrupts every downstream check. Flagging the duplicate-cards case is the senior signal: real-world inputs sometimes have data-quality issues, and 'I'd validate or trust the contract' is the right framing.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the bounds, and what does this generalize to?
sections.say:
"Time is O(1) — the hand is fixed at 5 cards. Every loop runs at most 5 times, the sort is on at most 5 elements, the ladder is at most 10 checks. The bound is the same whether you think of it as O(n) for n=5 or just O(1) constant.

Space is also O(1) — the counts object has at most 5 keys, the sorted arrays are at most 5 elements.

The interesting analysis isn't asymptotic — it's about the *structure*: feature extraction (group counts + flush + straight) followed by a top-down classification ladder. The same shape shows up in any rule-based classifier — fraud-scoring rules engines (extract features from a transaction, walk a priority-ordered rule list), spam classifiers before ML took over, even ESLint-style linting (parse the AST once, walk rules in priority order). If you wanted me to extend: compare two hands for tie-breaking, you'd need to surface the *kicker* — the high cards within the category. That's another sort-and-compare on the rank indices, layered on top of this category check."
sections.why: Saying 'the interesting analysis isn't asymptotic, it's structural' is the senior framing — you're acknowledging that O(1) is the trivial answer and pivoting to what the interviewer probably actually cares about (clean decomposition). The rules-engine / fraud-scoring analogy is the transfer move — it proves you see this as a *template* for any feature-extract-then-classify problem, not a poker-specific trick. The tie-breaker extension hints at the next level of poker logic without getting lost in it.

walkthrough.intro: Step through rankHand on three hands — a royal flush, a wheel straight (ace-low special case), and a full house. Watch the parsed ranks/suits, the count histogram, and the straight/flush flags before the ladder of `if` checks fires.
trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter rankHand(cards) — cards=${JSON.stringify(cards)}`, state: { cards } };
yield { line: 2, label: `order = '${order}' — index = rank strength (0=2, 12=A)`, state: { cards, order } };
yield { line: 4, label: `parse ranks (normalize '10'→'T') → ${JSON.stringify(ranks)}`, state: { cards, order, ranks } };
yield { line: 5, label: `parse suits (last char of each card) → ${JSON.stringify(suits)}`, state: { cards, ranks, suits } };
const idx = ranks.map(r => order.indexOf(r)).sort((a, b) => a - b);
yield { line: 6, label: `idx = ranks→order-positions, sorted asc → ${JSON.stringify(idx)}`, state: { cards, ranks, suits, idx } };
yield { line: 7, label: 'init counts {} (rank histogram)', state: { cards, ranks, suits, idx, counts: {} } };
yield { line: 8, label: `count '${r}' → ${counts[r]}`, state: { cards, ranks, suits, idx, counts: { ...counts } } };
const groups = Object.values(counts).sort((a, b) => b - a);

yield { line: 10, label: `groups = counts.values sorted desc → ${JSON.stringify(groups)} ([4,1]=four, [3,2]=full-house, [2,2,1]=two-pair, …)`, state: { cards, ranks, suits, idx, counts: { ...counts }, groups } };
yield { line: 11, label: `flush? every suit === '${suits[0]}' → ${flush}`, state: { cards, ranks, suits, idx, groups, flush } };
let straight = idx.every((v, i) => i === 0 || v === idx[i-1] + 1);
yield { line: 12, label: `straight? idx all consecutive → ${straight}`, state: { cards, ranks, suits, idx, groups, flush, straight } };
if (!straight && ranks.includes('A') && ranks.includes('2') && ranks.includes('3') && ranks.includes('4') && ranks.includes('5')) {
yield { line: 14, label: `wheel-straight override: A-2-3-4-5 all present → straight = true`, state: { cards, ranks, suits, idx, groups, flush, straight } };
yield { line: 14, label: `no wheel-straight override (straight already ${straight} or not A-2-3-4-5)`, state: { cards, ranks, suits, idx, groups, flush, straight } };
yield { line: 15, label: `--- ladder check (top-down, first match wins) ---`, state: { cards, groups, flush, straight, idx } };
yield { line: 16, label: `straight && flush && idx[0]===${order.indexOf('T')} ('T') → royal-flush`, state: { cards, groups, flush, straight, idx, returns: 'royal-flush' } };
yield { line: 16, label: `royal-flush? straight=${straight}, flush=${flush}, idx[0]=${idx[0]} (need ${order.indexOf('T')}) → no`, state: { cards, groups, flush, straight, idx } };
yield { line: 17, label: `straight && flush → straight-flush`, state: { cards, groups, flush, straight, returns: 'straight-flush' } };
yield { line: 17, label: `straight-flush? straight=${straight}, flush=${flush} → no`, state: { cards, groups, flush, straight } };
yield { line: 18, label: `groups[0]===4 → four-of-a-kind`, state: { cards, groups, returns: 'four-of-a-kind' } };
yield { line: 18, label: `four-of-a-kind? groups[0]=${groups[0]} → no`, state: { cards, groups } };
yield { line: 19, label: `groups[0]===3 && groups[1]===2 → full-house`, state: { cards, groups, returns: 'full-house' } };
yield { line: 19, label: `full-house? groups=[${groups.join(',')}] → no`, state: { cards, groups } };
yield { line: 20, label: `flush=true → flush`, state: { cards, groups, flush, returns: 'flush' } };
yield { line: 20, label: `flush? ${flush} → no`, state: { cards, groups, flush } };
yield { line: 21, label: `straight=true → straight`, state: { cards, groups, straight, returns: 'straight' } };
yield { line: 21, label: `straight? ${straight} → no`, state: { cards, groups, straight } };
yield { line: 22, label: `groups[0]===3 → three-of-a-kind`, state: { cards, groups, returns: 'three-of-a-kind' } };
yield { line: 22, label: `three-of-a-kind? groups[0]=${groups[0]} → no`, state: { cards, groups } };
yield { line: 23, label: `groups[0]===2 && groups[1]===2 → two-pair`, state: { cards, groups, returns: 'two-pair' } };
yield { line: 23, label: `two-pair? groups=[${groups.join(',')}] → no`, state: { cards, groups } };
yield { line: 24, label: `groups[0]===2 → pair`, state: { cards, groups, returns: 'pair' } };
yield { line: 24, label: `pair? groups[0]=${groups[0]} → no`, state: { cards, groups } };
yield { line: 25, label: `no category matched → high-card`, state: { cards, groups, returns: 'high-card' } };

notes: Normalize '10' to a single character ('T') so rank ordering uses a simple string index.
The rank ladder must be checked TOP-DOWN: a full-house also matches three-of-a-kind, but we return the stronger category first.
Wheel straight (A-2-3-4-5) is the special case where the ace is low — handle it explicitly because indices wouldn't be consecutive otherwise.
Time O(1), Space O(1) — hand is always 5 cards; all loops and arrays are bounded by a constant.

alternates.label: Groups-signature dispatch table
alternates.when: Reach for this when an interviewer says 'can you make the ladder more declarative?' or you want to collapse the group-based categories into a single Map lookup. The same feature extraction (groups + flush + straight) feeds a string key like '4,1' or '3,2' that looks up the category in a table. Reads more like a config than control flow — easier to extend (add a new variant just by adding a row), harder to re-order accidentally. Flush + straight + royal still need explicit if-checks since they don't reduce to a pure group signature.
notes: The key insight: every group-based category has a unique sorted-counts signature, so `groups.join(',')` is a perfect-hash dispatch key — no need to compare element-by-element.

Flush, straight, straight-flush, and royal-flush can't go in the table because they don't depend on the groups signature alone — they cross over with [1,1,1,1,1]. Handle them explicitly above the dispatch.
Default branch (`|| 'high-card'`) handles the [1,1,1,1,1] non-flush, non-straight case — no signature, no flush, no straight means nothing matches.

options: Checking flush-based hands first lets the function skip computing the rank histogram entirely on those branches
The categories are ordered by strength — the first matching category wins, and royal/straight-flush are stronger than four-of-a-kind
A four-of-a-kind whose four cards share a suit must be reclassified as a straight-flush by Hoyle's rules
Four-of-a-kind shares the `groups[0]===4` shape with a straight-flush, so the more specific predicate must run first
questions.explain: Every ladder line is an early `return`, so the first match wins and the ordering has to encode hand strength. The overlaps are real: a royal flush also satisfies the plain `straight && flush` test, and a full house also satisfies the later `groups[0] === 3` — reorder either pair and the stronger hand is silently reported as the weaker one.

questions.q: What is `groups` if the hand is a full house?
options: [2, 2, 1] — the pair + pair + odd-rank-out is the structural fingerprint
[5] — all five cards share a single bucket because the full house collapses the histogram
[3, 1, 1] — the trips dominate; the pair is recorded as two singletons
questions.explain: `counts` is `{K:3, 2:2}` for KKK22, and `Object.values(counts).sort((a, b) => b - a)` yields `[3,2]`. `[2,2,1]` is two-pair and `[3,1,1]` is bare trips — the sorted histogram is the single value that separates all three.

questions.q: Why rewrite '10' to 'T' before indexing into '23456789TJQKA'?
options: `'10'.indexOf` in a single-char rank string returns -1, which would mis-sort the ten below the deuce
So every rank is a single character — index lookup and sorting stay simple
`String.prototype.slice(0, -1)` returns the full string when the slice length is 2, so '10H' would parse as '10H' instead of '10'
The order string `'23456789TJQKA'` uses 'T' specifically because '10' would collide with the '1' suit-prefix used in some decks
questions.explain: `ranks` feeds both `order.indexOf(r)` and the `counts` keys. Left as `'10'`, `order.indexOf('10')` is `-1` — sorting below the deuce and breaking the consecutive-index straight check — so the fix is making every rank exactly one character.

questions.q: How is a flush detected from the parsed `suits` array?
options: Three or more matching suits — the standard 'majority-suit' flush rule
At least one suit appears twice — a single pair of same-suit cards establishes the flush flag
The set of unique suits has size 1 OR 2 — same-color (red/black) qualifies as a flush
questions.explain: `suits.every(s => s === suits[0])` compares every suit against the first, so the flag is true only when all five match. Majority-suit and same-colour are not flushes, and neither would survive that predicate.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the flush + four-of-a-kind detection.

blanks.hint: project each card to its rank
fallback when key not yet present
compare each suit to the first

L3.prompt: Implement rankHand(cards). Log ranks for: royal flush (TS-AS spades), four kings, full house (KKK + 22), wheel straight (A-5 mixed), pair of nines.
hints: Normalize '10' to a single character first — indexing into a rank string then becomes trivial.
Build a rank histogram and sort counts descending. `[4,1]` = four-of-a-kind, `[3,2]` = full-house, `[2,2,1]` = two-pair.
Check the categories TOP-DOWN: a full house also matches three-of-a-kind, but royal/straight-flush beat everything.
